knowledge/tools/crm-and-revops-stack-202.title: CRM and RevOps Stack 2026
knowledge/tools/crm-and-revops-stack-202.description: A practical guide to selecting and implementing CRM and revenue operations tools for small teams and solo founders, focusing on viable category leaders rather than exhaustive vendor lists. The core CRM decision hinges on fit (SMB vs. enterprise), sales motion (pipeline-first vs. marketing-led), and technical team comfort, with pricing ranging from free to $800+/seat/month across platforms like HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, and Attio. Critical implementation rules: don't run multiple CRMs (data drift occurs within 6 weeks), migration takes 2–6 weeks of manual data hygiene despite easy technical transfer, and all standard CRMs share a four-object model (Account, Contact, Opportunity, Activity) plus custom fields. Use this framework to eliminate false choice between vendors and focus on migration risk and scaling ceilings rather than feature shopping.
knowledge/tools/crm-and-revops-stack-202.summary: Prescribes the 4+N data model (Account→Contact→Opportunity→Activity + custom objects) as the architectural foundation for small-team revenue stacks, preventing the common failure of contacts-only systems that lose buying-committee visibility and forecasting. The paramount operational rule: consolidate on a single CRM (HubSpot $0–$800+/mo, Salesforce $25–$330+/mo, Pipedrive, Attio, Close, Folk) because parallel systems fail within 6 weeks due to data drift; migration takes 2–6 weeks.

knowledge/tools/fastapi.md.title: FastAPI
knowledge/tools/fastapi.md.description: FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building REST APIs with automatic OpenAPI documentation, Pydantic-based validation, and native async support. Built on Starlette (ASGI) and Pydantic v2, it offers async-first performance comparable to Node.js/Go, with automatic request/response validation from type hints and auto-generated Swagger UI documentation. It provides clean dependency injection for databases and auth, supports streaming responses and background tasks with minimal boilerplate. FastAPI has become the dominant choice for AI/ML backends due to its performance, developer experience, and tight Python type system integration—particularly valuable for LLM streaming APIs and complex validation.
knowledge/tools/fastapi.md.summary: FastAPI is an async-first Python REST API framework (built on Starlette + Pydantic) with automatic OpenAPI documentation from type hints and full request-to-response validation; it dominates AI/ML API backends because its performance is comparable to Node.js/Go while providing end-to-end type safety and Python ecosystem integration.

knowledge/tools/fastmcp.md.title: FastMCP
knowledge/tools/fastmcp.md.description: FastMCP is the standard Python framework for building MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers and clients, maintained by Prefect and downloaded approximately 1 million times daily. It auto-generates JSON schemas, validation, and MCP protocol boilerplate directly from Python type hints and docstrings, enabling servers to be declared via simple decorators like `@mcp.tool`. FastMCP supports three core pillars—servers (exposing tools, resources, and prompts), interactive apps, and clients—plus production features including OAuth 2.0 authentication, response caching, and multiple transports (stdio, HTTP/SSE, WebSocket). It eliminates significant boilerplate compared to the raw MCP SDK and powers approximately 70% of MCP servers across all languages, making it the dominant framework for MCP development.
knowledge/tools/fastmcp.md.summary: FastMCP is the standard Python MCP framework powering ~70% of servers by auto-generating JSON schema, validation, and protocol boilerplate from type hints and decorators; version 1.0 integrated into the official SDK with ~1M daily downloads and maintained by Prefect.

chunk_summaries.1.0: Chunk 1.0 introduces FastMCP as Prefect's standard Python framework for building MCP servers and clients, covering its three core pillars (servers, apps, clients), minimal server example, and key features including decorator-based tools, resources, prompts, authentication, caching, and transport protocols.

knowledge/tools/llama-cpp.md.title: llama.cpp
knowledge/tools/llama-cpp.md.description: llama.cpp is an open-source C/C++ library for efficient LLM inference on diverse hardware, from laptops to workstations, with minimal dependencies. It uses the GGUF binary format storing model weights, tokenizer, and metadata, with quantization schemes ranging from Q2_K (~2.6 bits) to F16 (16 bits), where K-quants provide per-layer adaptive quantization for superior quality. Hardware support spans CPU with SIMD optimizations, NVIDIA CUDA, Apple Metal, AMD Vulkan/ROCm, and OpenCL, with hybrid CPU+GPU offloading for models exceeding GPU VRAM. It enables practical local LLM inference with state-of-the-art performance and serves as the inference backend for Ollama, making it essential for on-device deployment scenarios.
knowledge/tools/llama-cpp.md.summary: llama.cpp is a C/C++ library for efficient LLM inference using GGUF format (single-file binary with quantized weights and metadata) and K-quants—adaptive per-layer quantization where Q4_K_M (~4.5 bits) is the recommended quality/VRAM tradeoff. It supports CPU SIMD, CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, and hybrid GPU/CPU offloading, and serves as Ollama's inference backend.

knowledge/tools/ollama.md.title: Ollama
knowledge/tools/ollama.md.description: Ollama is a local LLM inference server wrapping llama.cpp with a Go-based REST API, enabling Docker-like model management for open-weight language models on consumer hardware. It runs on localhost:11434 (11435 on VCO), supports GPU backends (CUDA, Metal, ROCm), uses quantized GGUF models, and processes requests sequentially with a REST API for completions, chat, embeddings, and model management via Modelfile format. Ollama supports streaming responses, tool calling (llama3.2+, qwen2.5+), vision/multimodal capabilities, structured JSON output, and Anthropic Messages API compatibility (v0.14+). This enables on-device inference without cloud dependencies, making it ideal for agentic tasks; 14B–32B+ models are recommended for production agents.
knowledge/tools/ollama.md.summary: Ollama is a Go-based REST API server wrapping llama.cpp that provides Docker-like model management for running quantized GGUF models locally on consumer hardware; its critical limitation is sequential request processing with no native concurrency or batching, making vLLM preferable for multi-user production deployments.

chunk_summaries.1.0: Ollama chunk 1.0 covers the local LLM server's core architecture (Go-based llama.cpp wrapper), REST API endpoints, model management via Modelfile, and available models including qwen3-coder, llama3.2:3b, and specialized embeddings models.

knowledge/tools/scientific-python-stack-.title: Scientific Python Stack 2026
knowledge/tools/scientific-python-stack-.description: A 2026 survey of Python libraries scientists actively use, organized by purpose—numerical computing, array containers, dataframes, and visualization. NumPy 2.0+ and SciPy provide the numerical core; Polars (Rust-backed) is now the default for new DataFrame code, delivering 3-30× faster performance than pandas; xarray+dask handle labeled n-dimensional arrays; JAX enables differentiable scientific computing. Zarr v3 and DuckDB offer modern alternatives for chunked, compressed storage; Narwhals abstracts across pandas/Polars/PyArrow to avoid conditional logic. This landscape matters because the 2026 ecosystem reflects modernization around lazy evaluation, out-of-core workflows, array-API standardization, and cross-language interoperability—guiding scientists to the right tool per workload.
knowledge/tools/scientific-python-stack-.summary: 2026 scientific Python stack: Polars replaces pandas as the default dataframe choice for new code, DuckDB becomes the standard for larger-than-RAM tabular analysis, NumPy 2.0+ serves as the numerical baseline, with xarray/zarr for labeled n-D arrays and array-API enabling cross-library compatibility.

knowledge/tools/terraform-opentofu.md.title: Terraform and OpenTofu (Infrastructure-as-Code)
knowledge/tools/terraform-opentofu.md.description: Terraform and OpenTofu are declarative Infrastructure-as-Code tools that describe desired cloud resources in HCL and automatically reconcile real infrastructure to match that state. Both share the same HCL language and 1000+ provider ecosystem (AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes, etc.); OpenTofu (Linux Foundation fork, Jan 2024) adds state encryption and early-evaluation variables after HashiCorp re-licensed Terraform under BUSL. The core workflow chains write HCL → init → plan → apply, with a remote state file (S3, GCS, or HCP) as the source of truth; plan diffs use symbols: + (create), ~ (update), -/+ (destroy+recreate—risky for stateful resources), and - (destroy). Use Terraform for HashiCorp commercial integration (HCP, Sentinel, Vault); use OpenTofu for OSS-only, state encryption, or BUSL concerns. Remote state with locking is mandatory in production.
knowledge/tools/terraform-opentofu.md.summary: Terraform and OpenTofu (Linux Foundation fork after BUSL re-license, Jan 2024) are HCL-based declarative IaC tools reconciling desired vs real infrastructure via plan/apply loops against a state file, ~90% compatible with OpenTofu adding native state encryption. Remote state with atomic locking is mandatory for multi-user production; `-/+` plan symbols (resource replacement) are the highest-risk operation, forcing destruction and recreation that destroys stateful data.

knowledge/tools/weaviate-usage-patterns..title: Weaviate Usage Patterns
knowledge/tools/weaviate-usage-patterns..description: Weaviate Usage Patterns describes practical implementation strategies for semantic search using Weaviate with Ollama embeddings, focusing on token budget constraints. The active embedding model (`qwen3-embedding:0.6b`, 1024-dim) supports ~10k tokens per chunk; queries and documents exceeding this budget must be truncated or chunked respectively, with Ollama silently truncating overages. Large documents use chunking with a shared `source_node_id` UUID and metadata (chunk_num, total_chunks) to preserve document relationships across multiple objects; small documents under budget store as single objects. Use these patterns to avoid truncation errors and maintain queryable document structure when token limits constrain embedding capacity.
knowledge/tools/weaviate-usage-patterns..summary: Weaviate with Ollama embeddings enforces per-model token budgets (10k for `qwen3-embedding:0.6b`, 4k for `snowflake-arctic-embed2`) that silently truncate oversize input; documents exceeding the budget must be chunked with shared metadata and a `source_node_id` UUID for deduplication during semantic search queries.

knowledge/tools/weaviate.md.title: Weaviate
knowledge/tools/weaviate.md.description: Weaviate is an open-source vector database that stores and searches high-dimensional vector embeddings with metadata filtering for semantic search and AI applications. It uses the HNSW algorithm for efficient approximate nearest neighbor search, supports property filtering through GraphQL and gRPC APIs, and includes knowledge graph capabilities with cross-references and relationship modeling. Schema design patterns support document chunks and knowledge nodes with rich metadata, and batch operations optimize performance for high-throughput workloads. Use Weaviate when building AI applications requiring semantic search with sub-100ms query times, knowledge graph features, and multi-tenant scalability.
knowledge/tools/weaviate.md.summary: Weaviate is an open-source vector database using HNSW algorithm for semantic search with sub-100ms queries, metadata filtering, and knowledge graph capabilities. Critical constraint: Ollama embedders silently truncate inputs beyond model-specific token budgets (e.g., ~10k for qwen3-embedding:0.6b), so chunking must target per-model limits via `Chunker.for_model()` rather than documented maximums.

chunk_summaries.1.0: Introduces Weaviate as an open-source vector database for semantic search, covering four core capabilities: HNSW-based similarity search, property filtering with GraphQL/gRPC, knowledge graph relationships, and multi-tenant namespace isolation.
